abstract: Dormancy is a reversible physiological state characterized by attenuated metabolism, reproduction, and feeding, yet the behavioral adaptations accompanying this state remain poorly understood. Here, we show that cold-induced dormancy in Drosophila melanogaster promotes the formation of large huddles ([≥]5 flies), which are rarely observed under warm conditions. Dormancy simultaneously shifts these huddles away from food, though the increased propensity to huddle persists even in the absence of food, revealing separable changes in huddling propensity and aggregation site selection. We further show that dormancy resets appetite, suppressing feeding despite energetic need. Neither starvation, unrestricted feeding, nor refeeding after starvation under warm conditions reproduced the dormancy-associated pattern of aggregation, suggesting that appetite suppression during dormancy extends beyond the range of normal warm hunger and satiety states. Increasing appetitive drive during dormancy nevertheless redirected aggregation toward food. A screen of appetite-regulating neuropeptide pathways identified Neuropeptide F (NPF) signaling as a regulator of both feeding and huddling during dormancy. Broad NPF activation increased feeding and suppressed huddling, whereas activation of an NPF-expressing fan-shaped body sub-population suppressed huddling without increasing feeding. Together, these findings establish huddling as a behavioral hallmark of Drosophila dormancy and demonstrate that the propensity to huddle can be experimentally dissociated from appetite-dependent aggregation site selection.
